population.note: FICTIONAL. There are about 276M adults. Current users are 36.4%, ≈100.5M. Ever-users are 48.5%, ≈133.9M. That leaves 12.1% (≈33.4M) who have used and are off now, and ≈142.1M who have never used. Cycling arithmetic: about 17 pts of current users are on a second or later course, and about 5 pts of the off-now group restarted and stopped again, so (17 + 5)/48.5 ≈ 45.4% of ever-users have cycled. That is slightly below 2034 because about 21M new starters since then, many of them new Medicaid, HRSA and AUD patients, have not yet had time to cycle. It still fits ~35% one-year persistence and 36–47% restart within a year. Ever-use rose 8.5 pts (limit 10.9) and current use rose 7.9. Age check: 18–29: 23.5% × 52M = 12.2M; 30–49: 41% × 92M = 37.7M; 50–64: 50% × 62M = 31.0M; 65+: 28% × 70M = 19.6M. Total ≈ 100.5M = 36.4%. The 18–29 band rose fastest (15.5 → 23.5%) because alcohol-use-disorder prescribing (guideline-endorsed Jul 2035, FDA-approved Aug 2036) and free provision at health centres reached young uninsured drinkers. About 2.6M adults are on the drug primarily for AUD. The 65+ band is held down by bone pauses and post-NAION stops, which cover about one in five older ever-users. Income thirds average (38 + 37 + 34.2)/3 = 36.4. The bottom-third gap narrowed from 7.5 to 3.8 pts as Medicaid grew 11.5 → 20.0M and 2.0M uninsured adults entered the HRSA free-provision programme. Imported and counterfeit users fell from 7.1M to ≈6.2M and are now concentrated in the 10 non-participating states and among undocumented and gig workers. The ≈142M never-users skew toward under-30s who neither drink heavily nor have obesity, people with contraindications, and a growing group who refuse on principle (the 'Unweighed' and 'Full Table' constituencies). Pediatric use is 1.4% of ≈73M ≈ 1.0M, mostly adolescents 12+ on Medicaid EPSDT; the adolescent bone readout is still only partly reported. About one child in two now lives with a parent who is on the drug or cycling off it.

access.public_coverage: FICTIONAL. The Metabolic Health and Recovery Act (May 2035) cut the Part D statutory obesity rate from $199 to $169 a month in exchange for a federal volume commitment. The $50 copay, BMI eligibility (≥30, or ≥27 with one comorbidity) and counselling visit are unchanged. AUD fills since the Aug 2036 approval run under the standard Part D benefit at the same $169 rate. Medicare pays for 21.1% of fills, ≈21.2M users: ≈19.0M aged 65+ and ≈2.2M disabled under-65. By indication that is ≈7.0M diabetes, ≈13.4M obesity and ≈0.8M AUD-only. Obesity-benefit spend: 13.4M × $169 × 12 ≈ $27.2B gross, less copays of 13.4M × $50 × 12 ≈ $8.0B, leaving ≈$19.1B net to the program. All Medicare incretin fills: 21.2M × $169 × 12 ≈ $43.0B gross. Medicaid: the Act pays a 100% federal match for 2036–2038 to states that adopt the CMS continuation standard. Nine more states joined (among them Georgia, Tennessee and South Carolina), bringing the total to 40 plus DC. Medicaid pays for 19.9% of fills, ≈20.0M users × $169 × 12 ≈ $40.6B gross before supplemental rebates. HRSA free provision: uninsured adults under 200% FPL with obesity or AUD get the 50 mg Wegovy pill or Foundayo free at federally qualified health centres in every state. HRSA buys at a contracted $119/month: 2.0M × $119 × 12 ≈ $2.9B, against a $3.0B annual appropriation. Public payers combined (21.2 + 20.0 + 2.0 = 43.2M, 43.0%) now exceed commercial (32.8%), so the public programme is the default payer.
access.generic_rest_of_world: India: 100+ semaglutide brands at $5–30/month, including generic 50 mg-equivalent oral semaglutide. The Telangana first-filer plant failed reinspection in 2035 and remains under US import alert. China: generic semaglutide, tirzepatide copies and 'research' retatrutide, with Chinese API still underlying most of the gray trade. Canada: generic semaglutide at CAD 45–70/month. Brazil, Mexico, Turkey and Egypt also have generics. US: the rival filers' mid-2035 settlement date was contingent on the first filer's 180-day exclusivity expiring or being forfeited. FDA found forfeiture in Nov 2035. The first filer and Novo challenged that finding, and a D.D.C. stay pending the ruling has kept every generic off shelves. Rivals hold tentative approvals, and analysts expect launch in 2037. Tirzepatide exclusivity runs later.
access.note: FICTIONAL. Managed decline. Prices moved down through negotiated channels: the $199 → $169 public rate; the $119 HRSA contract; and a Jan 2036 federal-portal maintenance cut of ≈$50, which reversed the 2033 increase, timed with the Act's volume commitment. Current cash/direct prices: injectable semaglutide and tirzepatide $199–279; 50 mg Wegovy pill $229; oral starting doses (Wegovy pill, Foundayo) still $149–150; retatrutide $379 direct and $1,549 list; amycretin $449; MariTide $499/month-equivalent. PBM net fell to ≈$175–190. Payer mix of ≈100.5M users: Medicare 21.1% (21.2M); Medicaid 19.9% (20.0M); HRSA free provision 2.0% (2.0M); commercial 32.8% (33.0M); cash/direct 18.0% (18.1M, including ≈4.3M 'calm' and 'focus' subscribers, down from 4.6M); imported/counterfeit 6.2% (6.2M). Sum = 100.5M = 100%. Employer coverage for weight management fell to 61% as some mid-size employers dropped it, citing Medicaid and HRSA as alternatives for low-wage staff. Mental-health parity law (MHPAEA) means plans that cover AUD medications cannot exclude semaglutide once it is approved for AUD, which opened a coded 'AUD door' into commercial coverage. ≈85% of covering plans remain gated, and about a third have tenure gates. The 503B exclusion and 503A injunction stand. Routes: ≈44% of users are on daily orals, up from 36%, because HRSA and most new Medicaid starts are pill-first.

on_market_classes: GLP-1 agonist, weekly injectable (semaglutide: Wegovy/Ozempic, incl. 7.2 mg)
GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GIP/GLP-1/glucagon triple agonist, weekly injectable (retatrutide, incl. 12 mg maintenance dose)
GLP-1 + amylin analogue combination, weekly injectable (CagriSema)
GIPR-antagonist/GLP-1 agonist antibody-peptide conjugate, monthly injectable (MariTide)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill incl. 50 mg; Rybelsus)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda, incl. generics)
indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: moderate-to-severe alcohol use disorder in adults (semaglutide injection 2.4 mg and Wegovy pill, FDA Aug 2036; ASAM/APA guideline-endorsed Jul 2035; label requires baseline BMI ≥22 and weight monitoring)
mainstream_offlabel_uses: 'calm', 'focus' and 'craving freedom' subscriptions (≈4.3M, slightly down), now routinely sold with 'holiday weekend' dosing calendars
alcohol reduction below AUD threshold ('sober-curious' dosing), especially among under-30s
smoking and vaping cessation (SHAPS trial still enrolling)
'metabolic health' / longevity regimens in concierge practices
pediatric under-12 use under specialist care
gray-market 'research' retatrutide among gym and physique users
gambling and compulsive-shopping craving reduction, still anecdotal
drugs.pipeline_note: FICTIONAL. No new class reached the market (next_gen_launch: none). The new_indications driver is met by an existing molecule: two 52-week phase 3 trials, one NIAAA-funded and one sponsored by Novo, showed a reduction of ≈2.1 heavy-drinking days a month versus placebo. ASAM and APA endorsed semaglutide for moderate-to-severe AUD in Jul 2035. The sNDA was filed Sep 2035 and approved Aug 2036 for the 2.4 mg injection and the Wegovy pill. Survodutide's MASH sNDA, under review at the start, was approved Oct 2035. Lilly's next-generation orals remain in development and unfiled. Bimagrumab combinations remain in phase 3 with no filing. The smoking-cessation SHAPS trial is still enrolling. Incretin market ≈$232B in 2036. US ≈$209B, computed from monthly paying-user revenue: Medicare 21.2M × $169 + Medicaid 20.0M × $169 + HRSA 2.0M × $119 + commercial 33.0M × ≈$185 + cash 18.1M × ≈$225 ≈ $17.4B/month × 12 ≈ $209B before Medicaid supplemental rebates. That is ≈94.3M paying users at an ≈$184 average net. Ex-US ≈$23B and eroding.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the most common effect and the leading cause of voluntary stops. Restart nausea is now common because drug holidays are widespread.
Rising in absolute numbers with the larger user base and the 65+ population.
No causal confirmation; absolute risk low. Alcohol co-use in AUD patients complicates attribution, and gray product confounds reporting.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; MDL litigation ongoing; the AUD label repeats the caution.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: ≈2.1M long-term older users meet sarcopenia criteria in Medicare claims, up from 1.6M. Lean mass is ~30–40% of loss in untrained users over 50.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Class label; body-composition monitoring in the high-efficacy labels; CMS annual DEXA requirement for long-term 65+ users unchanged.

safety_ledger.effect: Bone mineral density loss and fragility fracture
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: ≈9.5M users aged 65+ have more than 2 years' use. 9.5M × ~0.6%/yr baseline hip-fracture rate × 0.35 excess ≈ 20,000 excess hip fractures a year, against ~310,000 US total. The vertebral-fracture tail among cycling women 50–64 continues. DEXA waits are 10–14 weeks.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelling retained; bone endpoints required in filings; CMS 90-day bone-pause code unchanged. The DOJ civil case against Novo settled for $3.8B in Feb 2035 over sales-force messaging, with no new scientific finding.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Relative risk ≈1.7. ≈100M users × ~4/100,000 baseline × 0.7 excess ≈ 2,800 excess cases a year, mostly partial and permanent vision loss in one eye.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Class Warnings and Precautions (May 2034) carried onto the AUD label; MDL consolidated; not boxed.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No causal association, including in the AUD trial populations, which carry high baseline psychiatric risk.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia, 'the grey')
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: The 2032 retatrutide figures stand (~12% vs ~5% at 12 mg). The AUD trials collected SHAPS as a secondary endpoint and found a small mean shift that the sponsors call within normal range and critics call exactly the mechanism. There is still no randomised low-dose measurement in 'calm' subscribers. Self-directed drug holidays make exposure hard to measure.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: No label change. FTC consent orders stand. An NIH-funded low-dose study began enrolling in 2036.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Fewer forced stops than in 2033, but drug holidays and the PDC rules cause frequent short gaps. AUD patients who stop also report alcohol craving returning within weeks.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: CMS bone-pause code; the Seventh Circuit still has not ruled on the Indiana waiver.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Common in high-loss older users. Now also seen in AUD patients with pre-existing thiamine and folate deficits.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Professional guidance; ASAM guideline adds a thiamine screen. No FDA action.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~10 years; adolescent exposure; repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About fourteen years of follow-up. Adolescent bone data are partly reported, with one sponsor still on extension. Cycling still looks worse for bone than continuous use.
Imported or counterfeit users fell from ≈7.1M to ≈6.2M. Poison-centre GLP-1 calls are roughly flat since 2034. No contamination cluster has matched the scale of Nov 2033.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA import alerts maintained; seizures continue; the Safe Pens bill is still stalled; individuals still not prosecuted.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Upgraded to established on repeated seizure testing (0–300% of label). Mostly GI harms, plus hypoglycaemia in insulin users.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA warnings; NABP verified-pharmacy guidance; no new law.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: A few percent, higher at 12 mg; usually transient.

safety_ledger.effect: Falls and frailty-related injury in older users
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Fall-related ED visits remain elevated in 65+ users with more than 2 years' use. NAION is a minority cofactor.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Fall-risk screening mandatory in the Part D counselling visit.

safety_ledger.effect: Adverse body-composition cycling (fat-dominant regain after lean-dominant loss)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Fewer forced stops, but holiday-driven micro-cycling is unstudied. DEXA cohorts from the 2033 shortage confirm the pattern.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Joint guidance discussion; no regulatory action.

safety_ledger.effect: Heart-rate elevation at high triple-agonist doses
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Resting heart rate rises several bpm at 12 mg retatrutide; arrhythmia significance unclear.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Precautionary label; CV outcomes trial ongoing.

food_and_beverage.state: With 36% of adults on the drug, salty-snack volume keeps falling about 4% a year and confectionery about 5%. Protein and fortified dairy lead. Pill-first Medicaid starts in Georgia and Tennessee moved the discount grocers' value-pack strategy from 'regain' toward 'starter' protein shakes. A small heritage-baking revival rides the Full Table movement, with Memphis and Birmingham church-supply bakeries reporting their first growth in years.

alcohol.state: An eighth straight year of spirits volume decline, now near 4–5% a year, and beer down about 3%. AUD approval and sober-curious dosing hit heavy-consumer volume hardest, and that is where margin was. Distillers cut mid-price brands and consolidate warehouses in Kentucky. Bars in college towns report weaker late-night trade. Non-alcoholic formats keep growing. The industry is contracting, not collapsing.

restaurants.state: Traffic is flat and spend per cover is down about 12% from 2028 in high-uptake suburbs. Bar revenue is the weakest line. 'Full table' Sunday menus and unweighed family-style service have spread from Memphis and Houston into Atlanta and Charlotte as a backlash format.

apparel.state: The 'structured' and 'cycle' tiering persists. A small 'unweighed' label wave of size-inclusive, no-DEXA brands sells to women under 35. Resale sized for cycling keeps growing.

fitness.state: Growing. Medicare Advantage 'prescribed lifting' expands, and FQHCs pilot group strength classes alongside HRSA dispensing. The binding constraint is still staff who can train older lifters.

insurance.state: Employer weight-management coverage is down to 61%. As public programmes become the default payer, some employers drop coverage, while parity law forces AUD coverage. Pharmacy trend slowed to about +6% as net price fell. Gated and tenure designs persist. Fully insured plans in Texas and Tennessee can no longer price premiums off kiosk weights; self-insured ERISA plans can. Life insurers still price untreated BMI ≥30.

pharma.state: Volume is up about 29% over two years and average net price down about 8%. Lilly leads in injectables and Foundayo. Novo, after its $3.8B settlement and Corporate Integrity Agreement, wins the public and HRSA pill contracts and the AUD indication. Amgen's MariTide grows in the top third. The generic is still held up by a court stay.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Still income, but less sharply at the bottom. A free HRSA pill or a Medicaid script produces the soft 'pill body' that used to mark the middle. Trained, DEXA-verified shoulders still mark the top. The newest signal is refusal. A visibly unmedicated, comfortable larger body, especially in women under 35 and in Black church communities in Memphis, is now read as a stance rather than a lapse.
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: The use gap narrowed to 38% versus 34.2% across income thirds, and the import-pen body became rarer in the nine new Medicaid states. The body-composition gap persists: coaching and DEXA remain private goods. Women 50–64 who cycled through 2033 still carry the fat-dominant regain pattern.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Protein-first meals are the default among users. The backlash made the unweighed meal explicit. 'Full Table Sunday', started by Black Baptist congregations in Memphis, now runs in about 4,000 churches. Hosts ask guests not to dose that weekend, and many comply with a planned holiday.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Profiles list 'on', 'off', 'holidaying' and now 'Unweighed'. 'On for drinking' is a new and slightly guarded disclosure. Couples schedule dose holidays around anniversaries and trips.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Contested again. Insured professionals treat appetite as managed. The public programmes have made it something the state manages, which the 'natural' right calls the government pill. Fat-acceptance revivalists call appetite a right, and churches call it fellowship. The Novo settlement gave all three a shared villain without making the drug less used.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: FICTIONAL. Measured figures are unchanged: ~12% versus ~5% at 12 mg retatrutide, and a small SHAPS shift in the AUD trials. Self-report has moved: a 2036 national survey of users finds 38% say the drug 'turns down things I enjoy' and 41% took at least one deliberate drug holiday in the past year, most often for weddings, holidays or creative work. For 2.6M AUD patients the blunting is the therapeutic aim. For 4.3M 'calm' subscribers it is the product. For everyone else it is a complaint.
interior_life.framing: Treatment in addiction medicine, side effect in obesity clinics, character in conversation. 'The grey' is a common noun. Late-night hosts do holiday jokes, pharmacists counsel on restart nausea, and 'calm' brands sell holiday calendars.
interior_life.effect_on_work: 'Focus' reimbursement is quietly pulled from some lifestyle catalogues after the backlash, though most large employers keep it. Tenure gates still bind warehouse and call-centre workers in the 10 non-participating states. Elsewhere Medicaid and HRSA weaken metabolic tenure. EAPs now route drinking cases to the AUD indication. Pilots and safety-sensitive workers avoid the AUD code because FAA and DOT treat the diagnosis as reportable, so they seek obesity coding instead.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: Musicians and writers openly holiday for tours and deadlines, and 'holiday records' is a marketing phrase. Bar culture among under-30s thins out, and day-time sober venues grow. Documentary interest shifts from pen sellers to the Full Table churches.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Planned dose holidays before anniversaries are routine. Sex therapists treat the restart-nausea week as a known pattern. In AUD households, partners describe relief and flatness together.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: The 2035 Act passed with votes from both parties: Republicans framed it as addiction policy and Democrats as access. The backlash splits by party. The 'natural' and religious right attacks government pills and kiosk weights, while fat-acceptance and anti-pharma activists on the left cite the Novo settlement. State kiosk-data laws are the only legislative win, and ERISA blunts them.

state.regulatory_posture: FDA is data-demanding: it approved the AUD indication on two phase 3 trials, approved survodutide for MASH, and found the first filer's exclusivity forfeited, now stayed in court. DOJ secured a $3.8B Novo False Claims Act settlement over bone-risk sales messaging, with a five-year Corporate Integrity Agreement. FTC consent orders on 'calm' marketing stand. There are still no importation or authentication laws.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: The Metabolic Health and Recovery Act (May 2035) did four things. It cut the public rate to $169. It pays a 100% federal Medicaid match for 2036–2038 to states that adopt the continuation standard, which nine joined (40 plus DC). It funds HRSA free provision at $3.0B a year for uninsured adults under 200% FPL with obesity or AUD (≈2.0M served). It extends the $169 rate to AUD fills. There is no individual mandate.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: The CMS continuation standard is unchanged and now covers 40 state programmes plus DC, so about 9M more people verify weights at kiosks. HRSA free provision requires a clinic weight or AUDIT-C check every six months, not the full standard. Texas and Tennessee bar kiosk weights in fully insured premiums, but self-insured plans continue under the 30% wellness allowance. PDC ≥80% counts holidays as misses.
state.workforce_or_military: Large fleets keep visual-field checks for medicated drivers over 50. FAA and FMCSA treat an AUD diagnosis as reportable, which pushes coding toward obesity. Army accession policy is still contested; Air Force waivers continue.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: Chinese API and Indian finished product still supply most of the 6.2M-user gray market. Section 232 tariffs remain. The Telangana import alert remains a bilateral irritant. HRSA's pill contract requires US fill-finish, which manufacturers cite to justify tariff relief requests.

events.event: Novo Nordisk agrees to pay $3.8B to settle the DOJ False Claims Act case. Unsealed emails show sales managers coached reps to steer Medicare prescribers away from DEXA referrals and to describe bone loss as 'not established'. The company signs a five-year Corporate Integrity Agreement, and FDA says no label change is warranted

Congress passes the Metabolic Health and Recovery Act. It cuts the Part D statutory incretin rate from $199 to $169 in exchange for a volume commitment, offers a 100% federal Medicaid match for 2036–38 to states that adopt the continuation standard, and funds $3.0B a year for free pills at community health centres for uninsured adults with obesity or alcohol use disorder

Addiction-medicine and psychiatric societies endorse semaglutide for moderate-to-severe alcohol use disorder after two 52-week trials show about two fewer heavy-drinking days a month. Employee assistance programmes begin routing referrals within weeks

Nine more states, including Georgia, Tennessee and South Carolina, start incretin coverage under the 100% match, and the federal portal cuts maintenance prices by about $50. Medicare, Medicaid and health centres together now pay for more GLP-1 fills than employers, a first

About 30,000 people join a 'Full Table' march in Memphis led by Black Baptist pastors and 'Unweighed' fat-acceptance organisers. Texas and Tennessee then bar kiosk weights in fully insured premiums, a law self-insured employer plans are exempt from

FDA approves semaglutide for alcohol use disorder, and parity law forces employer plans that cover addiction drugs to include it. The same month a national survey finds 41% of users took a deliberate 'drug holiday' last year and 38% say the drug dulls pleasure

open_tensions: The generic is stayed in court until at least 2037, so public programmes now buy most of the volume at a negotiated brand price. If generics arrive, the $169 statutory rate and the HRSA contract will be above market, and Congress will have to reopen a law it just passed.

Drug holidays are now mainstream, but the CMS continuation standard counts them as missed days. About 20M Medicaid users and 13M Medicare obesity users must choose between the Sunday table and their PDC, and two misses still suspend coverage for six months.

The AUD indication makes reward blunting the therapy, while 4.3M 'calm' subscribers take a lower dose of the same thing for no indication. FAA and DOT reportability pushes safety-sensitive workers to code obesity instead of AUD, so the addiction data are undercounted from the start.

The bone bill keeps growing: about 20,000 excess hip fractures a year land on Part A while Part D just bought more volume at a lower rate. The Novo settlement penalised the messaging but changed no science, and the backlash coalition now treats every DEXA wait as proof.
still_true: No FDA-approved generic semaglutide or tirzepatide is on the US market; generic_us remains false.

The CMS continuation standard is unchanged: ≥80% PDC, verified six-monthly weights, 5% response or clinician override, annual DEXA for long-term 65+ users, the 90-day 'bone pause' code, and a 6-month suspension after two misses.
Part D obesity-benefit eligibility (BMI ≥30, or ≥27 with one comorbidity), the counselling visit and the $50 beneficiary copay are unchanged.
Oral starting doses (Wegovy pill, Foundayo) are still $149–150 a month cash through the federal direct-pricing portal and manufacturer direct channels.
The FTC consent orders still bar 'calm' and 'focus' brands from making anxiety-treatment claims, and the Safe Pens authentication bill is still stalled in Congress.

prose.headline: Uncle Sam Now Buys America's Appetite: Free Pills at the Clinic, Holidays at the Church Supper
prose.world_in_600_words:
At the end of 2036 a little more than one American adult in three is on an incretin drug, and for the first time the government pays for more of it than employers do. That was not the plan of any single person. It is the sum of a negotiated price cut, a federal match generous enough that nine reluctant states took it, and a line item that puts free pills on the shelves of community health centres from Memphis to Fresno.

The law that did it passed in May 2035, after a winter in which Novo Nordisk paid $3.8 billion to settle the government's case over how its sales force talked about bones. The emails were bad. Managers told reps to call fracture risk unproven and to keep older patients away from scans. The settlement changed no label and no science, but it changed the bargaining. The statutory Medicare rate dropped from $199 to $169 for a guarantee of volume. The federal portal cut maintenance prices by about fifty dollars, which undid the 2033 increase. Brands still cost $150 to $300 a month at the counter, and the generic that was supposed to arrive in 2035 is held up by a court stay. Access is still rationed. The rationing is just done by a different payer.

The largest new group of users is not who most people expected. Since summer 2035, addiction psychiatrists have prescribed semaglutide for alcohol use disorder on the strength of two year-long trials, and the FDA approved it in August. Employee assistance programmes route drinkers to it. Mental-health parity law means an employer that refuses to cover weight loss must still cover it for drinking, so coding has become strategic. Pilots and truck drivers, for whom an alcohol diagnosis is reportable, ask to be coded for weight instead. Distillers are consolidating warehouses in Kentucky, and college-town bars are quiet by eleven.

The young are arriving fastest. Nearly a quarter of adults under thirty are on the drug now, many through health centres, many for drinking rather than weight. The bottom income third is closing the gap. Imported pens are rarer in Georgia and Tennessee than they were two years ago, though they still dominate in the ten states that stayed out.

What people talk about has changed too. Two years ago the flattening was something brands sold. Now it is what everyone complains about. Four users in ten took a deliberate holiday last year, skipping doses before a wedding, a tour or a family dinner so they could feel the cake. Pharmacists counsel on restart nausea. Comedians do the bit. The 'calm' subscription brands sell holiday calendars beside a word they are legally forbidden to call treatment. For the alcohol patients, the dullness is the point.

The backlash has a home address. In April about thirty thousand people marched in Memphis behind Baptist pastors and young fat-acceptance organisers, under one banner and for different reasons. The churches want Sunday dinner back. The organisers want the kiosks gone. A 'natural' wing on the right calls it the government pill. Texas and Tennessee responded by banning kiosk weights from insurance premiums, but the federal law that governs self-insured employers means most workers are untouched.

The machinery underneath has not moved. Medicare and forty state programmes still require eighty per cent of days covered, a verified weight every six months and a bone scan for older long-term users, and a holiday counts as a missed day. Twenty thousand excess hip fractures a year land on a part of Medicare that does not buy the drug. On the outside it looks like a public-health success, and in many ways it is one.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Renee Holloway sets the alarm for 5:10 because Kroger's pharmacy kiosk is quietest before shift change. She is fifty-six and a home health aide in Whitehaven, and she has been on TennCare's pill since January, when the state signed on. Her copay is four dollars. Today is verification day.

She steps on the platform in her socks. The screen thanks her and shows 6.8 percent, which is enough. A woman behind her in scrubs pretends not to look.

She works two clients in Hickory Hill. Mr. Dade, eighty-one, asks again whether his scan came back, and it has not. Twelve weeks, the clinic said. She helps him do the chair stands the therapist left on a laminated card.

At lunch she counts days in the calendar app the pharmacy gave her. She skipped Saturday and Sunday last month for her sister's anniversary dinner at New Direction Baptist, Full Table Sunday, and she can skip once more this month and stay over eighty. Pastor Givens doesn't tell anyone to stop the pill. He tells them to come hungry.

At four she drives her son Marcus to Riverside Community Health. He's thirty-one, uninsured, and since March he has taken the free pill for drinking. The nurse checks his AUDIT score and his weight and hands him the white bottle. In the car he says he hasn't wanted a beer in nine days. He says it the way you'd tell someone about a quiet street you used to live on.

That night she lays out Sunday's sweet-potato pies to thaw, and Saturday's pill beside them, and decides about it in the morning.

least_plausible_claims.quote: as Medicaid grew 11.5 → 20.0M and 2.0M uninsured adults entered the HRSA free-provision programme
least_plausible_claims.why: Mechanism/magnitude: Nine states, mostly non-expansion Southern ones with thin adult Medicaid rolls, are said to add 8.5M users (+74%) within about a year of the Jan 2036 start. Nothing shows enrolment or uptake large enough to produce that.

least_plausible_claims.quote: Texas and Tennessee then bar kiosk weights in fully insured premiums, a law self-insured employer plans are exempt from
least_plausible_claims.why: Mechanism: Two state legislatures pass binding laws within weeks of an April march. Texas meets in odd years, so this would need a special session, and none is shown.

least_plausible_claims.quote: The 18–29 band rose fastest (15.5 → 23.5%) because alcohol-use-disorder prescribing (guideline-endorsed Jul 2035, FDA-approved Aug 2036) and free provision at health centres reached young uninsured drinkers.
least_plausible_claims.why: Magnitude/mechanism: The 18–29 band gains about 4.1M users, but only ≈2.6M adults of all ages are on the drug for AUD and HRSA serves 2.0M in total. A moderate effect (≈2.1 heavy-drinking days a month) and a pre-approval label do not reach that number.

rationale.badness: Measured against 2026, this world carries 36% of adults on the drug and about 20,000 excess hip fractures and 2,800 NAION cases a year. It also has 6.2M gray-market users and a CMS standard that counts drug holidays as misses, plus tenure gates and kiosk-weight premiums that turn coverage into conditioning. Public expansion and the HRSA programme narrow the income gap (7.5 to 3.8 points) and ease inequality somewhat. The 38% reporting dulled pleasure and the undercounted AUD data (safety-sensitive workers coding obesity instead) keep autonomy and epistemic harms near 5–6. It is a recognisably harder society with new losers, not a refusal-level one.

Minor gaps remain: the AUD sNDA was filed Sep 2035 and approved Aug 2036, about 11 months and under the 12-month rule, and Medicare 65+ users are 97% of all 65+ users versus 90% in 2034.

least_plausible_claims.quote: The sNDA was filed Sep 2035 and approved Aug 2036 for the 2.4 mg injection and the Wegovy pill.
least_plausible_claims.why: magnitude: the candidate describes phase 3 trials, and the envelope allows approval no earlier than 12 months after filing. Sep 2035 to Aug 2036 is 11 months, so the approval comes a month too early.

rationale.badness: Against 2026 (3), this world keeps the inherited harms in full. About 20,000 excess hip fractures a year, about 2,800 NAION cases and 1.0M adolescents on the drug remain. Kiosk-weight surveillance now covers 40 state programmes plus DC, PDC rules count dose holidays as missed days, and tenure gates persist. 'The grey' is a common complaint with no randomised low-dose measurement. AUD coding is undercounted because FAA/DOT reportability pushes safety-sensitive workers to code obesity instead. Offsets are real: the use gap between income thirds narrows, imports fall to 6.2M, and AUD treatment and free HRSA pills widen access, so it is slightly better than the 2034 start but still a harder society with new losers.
rationale.plausibility: driver_fidelity: Every driver is visibly realised. The adoption delta is exactly +7.9, the Act and the $199 to $169 cut give managed decline, the 40-state Medicaid match and HRSA provision give public expansion and subsidy, the AUD indication is met by an existing molecule, the DOJ settlement is the scandal, the Memphis march is the backlash, and the 38%/41% survey gives the mainstream complaint. next_gen_launch and safety_signal stay 'none'. mechanism: The chain from scandal to Act to rate cut to payer shift is shown, but several links are asserted. The scandal 'changed the bargaining' with no detail. The Medicaid jump is claim 1 and the Texas/Tennessee law is claim 2. The Act funds AUD provision before the Jul 2035 guideline endorsement. AUD patients (2.6M across all ages) cannot account for the 18–29 band rising 4.1M. The 65+ band rises 7 points while bone pauses and NAION stops are said to hold it down. magnitude: Headline figures sit inside the envelope (36.4%, ever-use 48.5%) and the age, payer-mix, Medicare and HRSA arithmetic reconciles. Flaws: the AUD approval at 11 months (claim 3), Medicare covering 19.0M of 19.6M users aged 65+ (97%, up from 90%), 'eighth straight year' of spirits decline when 2034 was already the seventh, and pharmacy trend of +6% against about 14% a year volume growth with net price down about 4% a year.

least_plausible_claims.quote: The 18–29 band rose fastest (15.5 → 23.5%) because alcohol-use-disorder prescribing (guideline-endorsed Jul 2035, FDA-approved Aug 2036) and free provision at health centres reached young uninsured drinkers.
least_plausible_claims.why: Mechanism: the world's own figures put AUD-primary users at ≈2.6M across all ages and HRSA at 2.0M for adults under 200% FPL with obesity or AUD. That cannot account for +4.1M users and an 8-point rise in the 18–29 band, and AUD approval came only in Aug 2036.

least_plausible_claims.quote: Mental-health parity law (MHPAEA) means plans that cover AUD medications cannot exclude semaglutide once it is approved for AUD, which opened a coded 'AUD door' into commercial coverage.
least_plausible_claims.why: Mechanism: MHPAEA requires parity in treatment limits, not coverage of a named drug. Plans can still manage formularies and gate use, and the world itself says ≈85% of plans remain gated. The 'door' is asserted rather than shown, and it sits oddly beside employer coverage falling from 64% to 61%.

least_plausible_claims.quote: showed a reduction of ≈2.1 heavy-drinking days a month versus placebo
least_plausible_claims.why: Magnitude and mechanism: this effect is modest, below the 2026 Lancet signal, yet it produced guideline endorsement within weeks and FDA approval within 11 months of the Sep 2035 filing. That is under the envelope's 12-month floor for a not-yet-filed phase 3 programme, and no AUD programme appears in the 2034 pipeline.

rationale.badness: Against the 2026 reference this is a recognisably harder society, and the 2034 harms are inherited in full: ≈20,000 excess hip fractures a year, ≈2,800 NAION cases, 6.2M gray-market users and counterfeit tablets. Autonomy is weighed down by PDC≥80% rules that count holidays as misses, kiosk-weight verification now covering 40 state programmes plus DC, and tenure gates. Reward blunting is a mainstream complaint, and AUD coding is distorted by FAA/DOT reportability. Inequality and access improved somewhat through Medicaid, HRSA and the narrowed income gap, which keeps this from rising past 6.
rationale.plausibility: driver_fidelity: every driver is visible in fields and events (current use 28.5→36.4, the $199→$169 managed decline, Medicaid and HRSA expansion, AUD approval, the $3.8B Novo settlement, the Memphis march, the Act's subsidy, the complaint framing), and nothing contradicts them. mechanism: several chains are asserted rather than shown, namely the 18–29 surge (claim 1), the MHPAEA coverage 'door' (claim 2), and a weak AUD effect that still yields rapid endorsement and approval (claim 3). Legislative responses such as the Texas and Tennessee kiosk bans also arrive very quickly. magnitude: current and ever-use sit inside the envelope, and the payer mix, Medicare, Medicaid and HRSA arithmetic, the $209B market and the age bands all reconcile. Minor gaps are Medicare's 19.0M aged 65+ against 19.6M total 65+ users, '21M new starters' against +24.3M ever-users, and AUD approval at 11 months, below the 12-month floor (claim 3).
rationale.generativity: The Renee Holloway day shows rather than explains: the 5:10 kiosk weigh-in, the 6.8% reading, the PDC calendar with skipped Full Table weekends, Mr. Dade's twelve-week DEXA wait, and Marcus's nine days without wanting a beer. The world supplies named places and institutions (Whitehaven, Riverside Community Health, New Direction Baptist, Kroger kiosks), and several more scenes are implied, such as pilots coding for obesity, church bakeries and college-town bars.
